subject: geography
title: Sense of Place & Lived Experience
welcome_lead: Distinguish insider, outsider and lived perspectives.
meta_desc: A-Level Geography adventure on sense of place, insider/outsider and lived experience.
final_note: Place is constructed through meaning, memory and media.

walkthroughs.body_html: Doreen Massey (1991) argued places are open, dynamic and connected to wider flows. Sense of place develops through repeated experience, memory and shared narratives. Hereford locals describe city centre very differently from tourists.

Insiders read landscape through tacit knowledge: which pub, which street name change, which slang. Outsiders rely on guides, signs, media. Both perspectives are valid but partial. Gentrification can turn insiders into outsiders in their own neighbourhood.

Ethnographic methods (observation, interviews) capture lived experience. Mass Observation Archive (since 1937) records everyday Britain. Qualitative approaches complement quantitative census data, revealing how places feel as well as how they measure.

mcqs.q: Why is HDI a better measure of development than GNI per capita?
options: Sustainable development means using only solar power.
Because HDI measures how happy people are.
HDI combines income, life expectancy and education, capturing quality of life — GNI per capita is just average income and hides inequality and non-economic wellbeing.
Because HDI is easier to calculate than GNI.
GDP measures the total wealth of every individual in a country.
Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs — balancing economic, social and environmental goals.
Sustainable development means using only solar power.
Sustainable development means stopping all economic growth.

mcqs.q: Why is GDP per capita a poor measure of wellbeing?
options: GDP measures the total wealth of every individual in a country.
Because HDI is easier to calculate than GNI.
GDP measures economic activity, not wellbeing. It ignores inequality, unpaid work, environmental damage and quality of life — high GDP can coexist with poor health, education or happiness.
A high GDP per capita means citizens are happy and well off.
